decisions.title: Publish from a snapshot taken after the last final whistle
decisions.question: Should the site keep serving the 2026-11-12 23:37 UTC snapshot while Thursday's game is finishing, or reconcile to the latest official standings before every publish?
decisions.scope: 1 new gate script + 1 workflow step; no data model change

options.label: Reconcile-then-publish (blocking gate)
options.buys: The standings page can never show a win total that contradicts a game the site itself lists as final.
options.costs: A publish can be delayed by minutes while the official page settles; a broken fetch blocks the site update.
options.risk: If nfl.com is unreachable, the publish fails closed and the site goes stale — needs a documented override.

options.label: Publish now, flag the lag
options.buys: No build risk; the site always updates.
options.costs: Two numbers on the same site disagree (snapshot says 136 games, the schedule page lists 137) and a reader has to notice the flag.
options.risk: Silent-looking inconsistency; a reader who ignores the flag makes a decision on a stale table.

options.label: Show both snapshots side by side until they agree
options.buys: Transparent and needs no new gate.
options.costs: Doubles the size of the standings table; readers must choose which row to trust.
options.risk: Presentation is longer than the problem deserves.

decisions.rec_why: The failure mode of B is a reader trusting a table that the site's own schedule page contradicts. The override for A is one documented switch, exercised only when the official fetch fails.
decisions.gate: Gate: a script fails the build if any club's W-L-T differs from the official page fetched in the same run, unless the run is flagged `official_unreachable`.

decisions.title: Retire the -110 price assumption before any strategy is presented as a candidate
decisions.question: Two leaderboards are live: one assumes -110 on every bet, the other uses observed prices. Which one should be the only one on the site?
decisions.scope: 1 renderer + 1 data file; no analysis rewrite

options.label: Observed-price board only
options.buys: Every scored bet carries the price the source recorded; the ROI is achievable by definition at that price.
options.costs: Parts of the file carry no price, so 1,902 of 6,653 priced-or-unpriced games are excluded and must be published as excluded.
options.risk: Smaller samples per rule; several rules fall below 200 bets and therefore cannot pass any gate.

options.label: -110 board only
options.buys: A much longer window (2005-2026) and bigger samples.
options.costs: Every ROI on the page is an assumption, not an observed return; a real book prices most of these at worse than -110.
options.risk: Overstates returns by construction; the assumption is documented but the headline number is not achievable.

options.label: Keep both, labelled and separated
options.buys: Continuity with earlier pages; both methodologies stay visible.
options.costs: Two rows can carry the same rule name and different ROI, which is the current state.
options.risk: Reader confusion; this is exactly what produced the conflicting numbers today.

evidence.note: S11 'Under in divisional games with total 47+' 4.2% (-110 board)
the closest rule is S09 'Under when the total is 40 or lower' at -7.9%

decisions.rec_why: A leaderboard competition is only meaningful if the number it ranks is a return someone could have earned. The -110 board can stay as a labelled sensitivity table, never as the headline.
decisions.gate: Gate: no strategy may appear in the headline table without a non-null average decimal price and a count of excluded bets on the same row.

decisions.title: Keep the published ranking rule and lock it with a test
decisions.question: The board is correctly ordered by the lower 95% ROI bound. Should that ordering be enforced by a test, or left to the renderer?

options.label: Rank by lower 95% bound of ROI
options.buys: Matches the published sentence; a lucky small sample cannot top the table.
options.costs: Every row currently shows a negative lower bound, so the top of the table is the 'least negative' strategy — honest but unflattering.
options.risk: A reader may read rank 1 as a winner. Needs an explicit 'no rule passes' banner above the table.

evidence.note: 'Ranked by the lower bound of the 95% ROI interval'

options.label: Rank by gates passed, and say so
options.buys: Zero code risk; matches what the table already does.
options.costs: A rule with a good gate count and a deeply negative ROI can outrank a rule with a better return.
options.risk: Ranks methodology compliance, not skill — the opposite of a competition.

decisions.rec_why: The order is right today and nothing protects it. A one-line assertion is cheaper than re-auditing the table next time it changes.
decisions.gate: Gate: a unit test fails if the rendered row order differs from the order of score_lower_ci_roi_pct.

decisions.title: Decide whether props stay projection-only or get a licensed price source
decisions.question: No prop market on the site has a price, so no prop bet can be scored. Is a priced prop feed in scope?
decisions.scope: 1 new data source + licence review; no code until a source exists

options.label: Stay projection-only, say so once
options.buys: Honest and free; nothing on the site implies a prop edge.
options.costs: Prop combos cannot enter the leaderboard; the 'single bet / parlay / prop combo' requirement stays partially met.
options.risk: The competition covers two of the three bet types the brief asks for.

evidence.note: 'UNVERIFIED / BLANK: no official or book-level price exists'

options.label: Add a licensed price feed
options.buys: Props become scoreable and the competition is complete.
options.costs: A commercial licence, a new collector, and a price-history store; none of that exists today.
options.risk: Licence cost and terms are commercial facts this repository cannot verify. Blank until quoted.

evidence.note: the NFL publishes standings, not prices

decisions.recommendation: A now, B only with a quoted licence
decisions.rec_why: Publishing a prop leaderboard without prices would be a fabricated edge. The blank is the correct output until a priced source exists.
decisions.gate: Gate: a prop bet may only be scored when its price is present and timestamped before kick-off.

decisions.title: Use club-published charts as the official fallback for 2nd/3rd/4th string
decisions.question: nfl.com publishes no depth chart (verified 404 today). Are the 32 club sites acceptable official sources for depth order?

options.label: Club sites, labelled per club
options.buys: 31 of 32 clubs are already scraped; the chart is the club's own publication, and several label it 'Unofficial'.
options.costs: Labels and update cadence differ by club; HOU could not be read.
options.risk: Two clubs may publish on different days, so a cross-team comparison can mix snapshots.

evidence.note: HTTP 200 body '404 - Flag on the Play'

options.label: Wait for an official league-wide chart
options.buys: One consistent source for all 32 clubs.
options.costs: No such page exists; the 2nd/3rd/4th-string requirement would stay unmet.
options.risk: Indefinite block on an explicitly requested feature.

decisions.rec_why: The club publishes the chart; citing the club and its own label is a stronger provenance claim than citing a third-party aggregator. The gap that matters is coverage, not authority.
decisions.gate: Gate: every depth row carries its club URL and the club's own chart date, or renders as an explicit blank.

decisions.title: Publish all 31 scraped clubs, not the 3 that reach the page
decisions.question: The scrape holds 31 clubs and 934 position rows, but the published chart page covers 3 clubs (KC, GB, SF). Why, and what should be published?

options.label: Render all 31 clubs from the existing scrape
options.buys: Closes the 2nd/3rd/4th-string gap for 31 clubs with data already in the repo and already sourced.
options.costs: A large page; needs a per-club filter or one page per club.
options.risk: HOU stays blank and must be labelled, not hidden.

options.label: Keep the 3-club sample
options.buys: No work.
options.costs: The site does not answer the question it was built to answer for 28 clubs.
options.risk: A reader assumes no other club has a chart.

decisions.rec_why: The data is already collected, hashed and sourced. Rendering it is a presentation change with no new claims.
decisions.gate: Gate: a coverage counter on the page prints captured clubs / 32 and names the clubs without a chart.

decisions.title: Separate 'no game designation yet' from 'healthy'
decisions.question: Mid-week, most clubs publish practice participation only. Should a blank game status be treated as available?
decisions.scope: 1 column + 1 rule in the availability model

options.label: Three-state column: Out / Questionable-family / No designation yet
options.buys: A reader can see that 'blank' means 'not published', not 'fit'.
options.costs: One more column; the attrition index needs a documented weight for the third state (it already uses 0.5/0.2 for practice-only).
options.risk: Any weighting is a modelling choice and must be labelled as a model weight, not an NFL statistic.

evidence.note: 9 rows carry a game status; the rest are practice-only

options.label: Keep the current single index
options.buys: One number per club, easy to scan.
options.costs: Collapses 'not published' and 'fit' into the same reading.
options.risk: A club that has not reported looks as healthy as a club with a fully cleared list.

decisions.rec_why: The distinction is the whole point of tracking injuries against a depth chart: the reader needs to know whether a starter is out or simply not yet designated.
decisions.gate: Gate: no cell may render blank; each renders 'No designation yet' with the source date, or the official value.

decisions.title: Publish inactive lists for games already played
decisions.question: Once a game kicks off, the official inactive list is the authoritative availability record. Is it in scope?
decisions.scope: 1 collector + 1 table; depends on a reachable official page

options.label: Add the official inactives page per week
options.buys: Turns 'questionable' into 'did not dress', which is what actually happened.
options.costs: The list is published about 90 minutes before kick-off and is per game, not per player.
options.risk: The nfl.com inactives article URL changes weekly; the collector must fail loudly rather than silently skip.

evidence.note: week-9 article linked from the injury page news rail

options.label: Leave it out
options.buys: No new dependency.
options.costs: Post-game availability analysis stays weaker than pre-game.
options.risk: None, other than the gap.

decisions.rec_why: Inactives are the only official record of who actually dressed; without them, 'Questionable' remains an unresolved category forever.
decisions.gate: Gate: an inactive row is only published with the game id and the official article URL it came from.

decisions.title: Make the market comparison explicit on every line
decisions.question: Own lines are published next to consensus closing lines. Should the page state where the market number comes from every time?

options.label: Every market cell links to its feed
options.buys: A reader can tell an observed price from a modelled one.
options.costs: Cells get a second link next to the official one.
options.risk: None identified.

options.label: One footnote for the whole table
options.buys: Cleaner table.
options.costs: A reader who screenshots one row loses the provenance.
options.risk: Same class of problem as the standings drift: provenance that lives far from the number.

evidence.note: market columns cite the nfl.com schedule page

decisions.rec_why: The brief asks for a source link on every row. A modelled market number presented without its feed is the one place the site currently breaks that rule.
decisions.gate: Gate: the link checker fails a table row whose market cell has no https source.

decisions.title: Define the reward pool before the first passing strategy
decisions.question: The competition promises rewards for top strategies. No official source publishes reward values. Should the pool be defined now or after a strategy passes?

options.label: Publish the reward spec as a formula with blank values
options.buys: The rules are fixed before anyone can win, which is the anti-cherry-picking argument.
options.costs: A document with blanks looks unfinished.
options.risk: A formula can still be tuned later; only a signed-off spec prevents that.

evidence.note: reward values not published by any official source

options.label: Wait until a strategy passes the gates
options.buys: No premature spec.
options.costs: At the current rate (0 of 12 rules pass) that could be a long wait, and the formula would then be chosen by the winner's shape.
options.risk: Any reward defined after the fact is a post-hoc selection.

decisions.rec_why: Publishing the formula before a winner exists is the cheapest way to make the competition credible. The values can stay blank until a human sets them.
decisions.gate: Gate: the reward page must show the formula version and the date it was frozen.

decisions.title: One entry point or six generations
decisions.question: The repo publishes six site generations (root dashboard, pages/, docs/, verified-lab/, referee/, lab/, dashboard/, research/, room/). Should the landing page route readers to one of them?

options.label: One landing page, every generation linked and labelled
options.buys: A reader sees one front door and can still reach every earlier build.
options.costs: The landing page must carry a 'what is this' line per generation.
options.risk: Six links invite comparison shopping between conflicting numbers.

options.label: Merge everything into one generation
options.buys: No conflicting numbers.
options.costs: Destroys independent implementations that cross-check each other, which is the repo's main quality signal.
options.risk: Loses the independent reproduction that caught the division-count bug.

decisions.rec_why: The independent builds are the reason several errors were caught. Keep them, but make the front door single and state which generation is authoritative for each table.
decisions.gate: Gate: every generation page carries a one-line 'authoritative for' statement.

decisions.title: Run the official-source audit as a required check, not an advisory one
decisions.question: The 34-check source audit exists but does not block a merge. Should it?

options.label: Make it a required check
options.buys: A hard mismatch stops publication; documented flags stay visible.
options.costs: A flaky nfl.com fetch can block a legitimate merge.
options.risk: Requires a documented override path with a recorded reason.

options.label: Keep it advisory
options.buys: No blocked merges.
options.costs: Every drift has to be spotted by a human reading the flag page.
options.risk: Today's NYG/WAS drift was found by hand, not by CI.

evidence.note: caught in this session by re-fetching

decisions.rec_why: An advisory audit is a report; a required audit is a gate. The brief asks for validation gates that block.
decisions.gate: Gate: the workflow is listed under required status checks and its failure message names the failing row.

decisions.title: Publish the sample definition next to every correlation
decisions.question: Correlation C1 reproduces in value (0.4309 vs 0.4312) but not in sample size (7103 vs 6975). What should a published correlation carry?

options.label: Sample definition + n + exclusion count on every figure
options.buys: A reviewer can reproduce n exactly, not just r.
options.costs: More columns.
options.risk: None identified.

evidence.note: n=7103, r=0.4309 with every row that has a spread and a result

options.label: Publish r with a confidence interval only
options.buys: Compact.
options.costs: n cannot be audited, so the interval cannot be checked.
options.risk: The width of the interval is the claim; without n it is unverifiable.

decisions.rec_why: The whole repository argues that an unreproducible number is not evidence. That has to apply to its own correlations.
decisions.gate: Gate: a correlation row without n and a filter description is a build failure.

decisions.title: Give the two index.html writers one owner
decisions.question: `pipeline/gen_site.py` writes `index.html` and the collect workflow commits it. `tools/build.py` also writes it and runs in the pull-request job, where its output is used only to check that the committed site would pass. Which one owns the file?

options.label: build.py stops writing index.html (writes legacy-site.html instead)
options.buys: One committed writer for the front door; the pull-request check then audits the page the site actually serves instead of a substitute.
options.costs: One line moves; the legacy page already exists.
options.risk: tools/verify.py reads index.html and needs the same file-list change; another session's generator changes shape.

options.label: Leave both, keep the CI replacement
options.buys: No risk today.
options.costs: The pull-request check keeps auditing a generated substitute, and any local or ad-hoc run of tools/build.py still overwrites the front door in the working tree.
options.risk: A regeneration in the wrong context silently republishes a page whose numbers come from a different data layer. This happened in the repository's own history.

decisions.rec_why: A front door with two authors will drift every time either runs. The fix is one line and the existing flag already documents it.
decisions.gate: Gate: a grep-based test fails if more than one renderer writes index.html.
